# `array`, `seq`, and `openArray`

Two collections that look alike can behave very differently. One has its size fixed when it is
written and never changes; the other can grow while the program runs. Picking wrong means hitting a
wall halfway through.

Nim pushes you to decide up front. An `array` has a fixed size and is stored in place; a `seq` has a
dynamic size and can grow. This chapter uses both, then introduces `openArray`: a single procedure
parameter that accepts either, without copying.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can write a fixed-size `array`, grow a `seq` with `add`, `insert`, and
`delete`, use the index `[^1]` for the last element, write an `openArray` parameter that accepts both
an `array` and a `seq`, and recognize an out-of-bounds index error.
:::

## `array`: fixed size

Save this as `main.nim`, then run it.

```{.nim}
var scores = [90, 75, 60]

echo "len: ", scores.len
echo "first: ", scores[0]
echo "last: ", scores[^1]

scores[1] = 80
echo "all: ", scores
```

```{.txt}
len: 3
first: 90
last: 60
all: [90, 80, 60]
```

`[90, 75, 60]` is an `array` literal; its type is `array[3, int]`. Indices start at `0`, so the last
element sits at `len - 1`. Nim offers a way to read from the back: `[^1]` means one from the end,
here the same as `scores[2]`.

The elements of an `array` may be changed one by one as long as the variable is a `var`. Declaring
`let scores` freezes the whole array, elements included.

## `array[N, T]` and default values

```{.nim}
var buffer: array[3, int]

echo buffer
buffer[0] = 7
buffer[2] = 9
echo buffer
echo "len: ", buffer.len
```

```{.txt}
[0, 0, 0]
[7, 0, 9]
len: 3
```

The type `array[3, int]` means three elements of type `int`. Without an initial value, Nim fills
every element with the element type's default: `0` for `int`, `""` for `string`. The length is part of
the type: `array[3, int]` and `array[4, int]` are two different types.

## `seq`: a size that can change

```{.nim}
var names = @["ada", "bob"]

names.add("cyd")

echo "len: ", names.len
echo "last: ", names[^1]
echo names
```

```{.txt}
len: 3
last: cyd
@["ada", "bob", "cyd"]
```

The `@` prefix turns an `array` literal into a `seq`, so `@["ada", "bob"]` has type `seq[string]`.
`add` appends one element at the end. A `seq`'s length is known while the program runs, so the number
of elements is not written into the type.

Note the last line: `echo` prints `@["ada", "bob", "cyd"]`, `@` included. That sign marks the value
as a `seq`, not an `array`.

## Inserting and deleting

```{.nim}
var numbers = @[10, 20, 30, 40]

numbers.insert(15, 1)
echo "after insert: ", numbers

numbers.delete(2)
echo "after delete: ", numbers

echo "first: ", numbers[0], " last: ", numbers[^1]
```

```{.txt}
after insert: @[10, 15, 20, 30, 40]
after delete: @[10, 15, 30, 40]
first: 10 last: 40
```

`insert(15, 1)` inserts the value `15` at index `1`, and everything after it shifts one place.
`delete(2)` removes the element at index `2`; the index is counted **after** the insert,
not before. Both change the length of the `seq`.

## An empty `seq` and gradual filling

```{.nim}
var squares: seq[int] = @[]

for i in 1 .. 4:
  squares.add(i * i)

echo squares
echo "len: ", squares.len
```

```{.txt}
@[1, 4, 9, 16]
len: 4
```

`@[]` is an empty `seq` with no elements. Being empty, its type cannot be inferred from its contents,
so the annotation is mandatory: `seq[int]`. After that, `add` is called repeatedly inside a loop.

## `openArray`: a parameter that accepts both

```{.nim}
proc total(values: openArray[int]): int =
  for value in values:
    result = result + value

let fixed = [1, 2, 3]
let dynamic = @[4, 5, 6]

echo "array: ", total(fixed)
echo "seq: ", total(dynamic)
```

```{.txt}
array: 6
seq: 15
```

`openArray[int]` accepts an `array` or a `seq` whose element type is `int`, without copying the
contents. This is the parameter kind used by `add`, `insert`, and many `std/` procedures. The
difference from `array` and `seq`: `openArray` works only as a parameter, not as a type you can store
in a variable or return from a procedure. A procedure that takes an `openArray` also cannot change
its length.

One note about copying: assigning an `array` or a `seq` to a new variable copies the contents
instead of sharing them. Changing the copy does not touch the original, unlike a `list` in Python.

## Index bounds and the out-of-bounds error

The valid indices for an `array` or `seq` of length `len` run from `0` to `len - 1`. A constant index
past the end is caught at compile time:

```{.nim}
let values = [10, 20, 30]

echo values[5]
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(3, 13) Error: conversion from int literal(5) to range 0..2(int) is invalid
```

Nim re-checks the index against the valid range (`0..2` for three elements). Since `5` does not fit
that range, the program is never built.

When the index is only known while the program runs, the compiler cannot help:

```{.nim}
let values = [10, 20, 30]
var index = 5

echo values[index]
```

```{.txt}
Error: unhandled exception: index 5 not in 0 .. 2 [IndexDefect]
```

The program compiles, then stops when it runs. `IndexDefect` is the exception raised for an
out-of-bounds index, and the message names the bad index along with the valid range. This behavior is
safer than C, which in the same case reads memory outside the array with no warning. The output above
is trimmed; the full output also contains a stack trace.

The check is on from the start, even when the program is compiled with `-d:release`. Only `-d:danger`
turns it off; after that the example above prints a random value from outside the array.

## Exercises

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

1. Create a `seq` holding three names, then insert a new name at the front without overwriting the
   first element.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   var data = @[1, 2, 3]
   data.delete(0)
   data.add(data[^1] + 1)
   echo data
   ```
3. Write a procedure `smallest(values: openArray[int]): int` that returns the smallest value, then
   call it with an `array` and with a `seq`.
4. `var x = @[]` fails to compile, while `var y: seq[int]` runs and its length is `0`. Explain why
   the two differ.
5. The code below fails. Fix it, then explain why the compiler rejected it:
   ```{.nim}
   var values = [10, 20, 30]
   values.add(40)
   ```

## Summary

- An `array` has a fixed size that is part of the type; a `seq` can grow and is built with `@[...]`.
- `[^1]` reads the last element; the only valid indices are `0` through `len - 1`.
- `add`, `insert`, and `delete` change the contents of a `seq`; `insert(item, index)` inserts,
  `delete(index)` removes.
- `openArray[T]` as a parameter accepts both `array` and `seq` without copying, but cannot be stored
  or returned.
- A constant out-of-bounds index is rejected at compile time; a runtime index raises `IndexDefect`.
